title: The Historian Who Sat Still
book: Sapiens: A Brief History of Humankind
author: Yuval Noah Harari
wiifm: Every business you run rests on things that exist only because people agree they do: a company, a pound, a regulator, a brand. Sapiens is the book that made millions of readers notice that, and it was written by a young medieval historian who taught himself to sit still and watch his own mind. You will follow Yuval Noah Harari from a bookish boyhood in Haifa to an Oxford doctorate, a meditation cushion and a first-year lecture hall in Jerusalem, and you will also hear plainly where the experts think he went too far.

b: Yuval Noah Harari was born on the twenty-fourth of February 1976 in Kiryat Ata, a small industrial town in northern Israel, and grew up in Haifa, a port city climbing up the slopes of Mount Carmel. His family were secular Jews with roots in Eastern Europe and Lebanon. His father was a state engineer in the arms industry, his mother an office administrator, and the boy was the sort who read everything and asked why about all of it.

He was clever enough to be put into a special programme for gifted children at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem by the age of eight. He has said that even as a child he was troubled by the big questions: why the world was the way it was, why there was so much suffering, and why the stories adults told him about nation and religion did not quite add up.

There was a private question too. He has said that he only realised he was gay at twenty-one, and has wondered aloud how he could have failed to notice something so basic about himself for so long. He took a lesson from it that runs through everything he later wrote. The mind is perfectly capable of hiding the most obvious facts from its owner, especially when the surrounding culture has a story that says those facts should not exist.
ch.cap: Young Yuval reads above Haifa's harbour at dusk

b: Harari studied history at the Hebrew University and then went to Jesus College, Oxford, where he completed a doctorate in 2002 under the historian Steven Gunn. His subject was narrow and specialised: the memoirs that soldiers wrote about war between roughly 1450 and 1600. For years he lived among knights, mercenaries and the stories fighting men told about themselves. Nothing about it suggested a global bestseller.

What changed him happened in 2000, while he was still a doctoral student. A friend persuaded him to try a ten-day silent retreat in Vipassana meditation, the method taught by S N Goenka. For ten days you do not speak. You simply observe the breath and the sensations of the body, hour after hour. Harari has said that he discovered how little control he had over his own mind, and how much of what he took for reality was in fact commentary that his mind added.

He has kept it up ever since, meditating for around two hours a day and taking a long retreat every year. Not long afterwards he met Itzik Yahav, who became his husband and later his manager. Remember the cushion, because Sapiens is in a sense a book written by a man practising that discipline on the whole species. He looks at our most precious beliefs and asks, quietly, which of these are sensations of the world, and which are stories we have told ourselves about it.
ch.cap: Harari meditates while ghostly knights drift away

ch.h: The lecture that grew into a book
b: Back in Jerusalem as a young lecturer, Harari was handed a job nobody senior wanted: the introductory course in world history for first-year students. Specialists usually teach their own period. He had to teach all of it, from the first humans to the internet, in a single year.

So he did what a good storyteller does with too much material. He stopped asking what happened and started asking what mattered. Out of that course came a Hebrew book, published in Israel in 2011, and in 2014 an English edition titled Sapiens: A Brief History of Humankind. It went on to sell tens of millions of copies in dozens of languages, with endorsements from Barack Obama, Bill Gates and Mark Zuckerberg.

The book is built around three revolutions. The Cognitive Revolution, around seventy thousand years ago, when our ancestors began to think and talk in new ways. The Agricultural Revolution, around twelve thousand years ago, when they started farming. And the Scientific Revolution, about five hundred years ago, which is still going on. Each one, he argues, changed not just what humans did but what kind of animal we are.
ch.cap: Harari teaches all of history to first-years

b: Harari opens by taking us down a peg. For most of their history, humans were unremarkable animals. Several kinds of human walked the earth at once: Neanderthals in Europe, Homo erectus in Asia, small island species on Flores, and our own kind, Homo sapiens, in East Africa. We were in the middle of the food chain, eating what lions left and cracking bones for marrow.

Then, he says, something happened to Sapiens. Somewhere around seventy thousand years ago our ancestors spread out of Africa and, within a few tens of thousands of years, the other humans were gone. Harari is honest that we do not know exactly how, and that the evidence for interbreeding with Neanderthals means some of them live on in our genes. But the result is plain: one human species remained.

His explanation is language, and not just any language. Many animals can say there is a lion by the river. Harari suggests our ancestors developed language partly to gossip, to keep track of who was trustworthy and who was sleeping with whom, which let bands grow to perhaps a hundred and fifty people. But the decisive leap was the ability to talk about things that do not exist at all.

He uses a rough number from the anthropologist Robin Dunbar: around a hundred and fifty people is about the largest group most of us can know personally. Beyond that, gossip runs out. To organise thousands, you need something that does not depend on knowing everyone, and that is where Harari's next idea comes in.
ch.cap: Early humans crack bones after the lions have fed

ch.h: Peugeot and the power of fiction
b: This is the heart of the book. You can never convince a monkey to give you a banana by promising it unlimited bananas after death in monkey heaven, Harari says. Only humans believe such stories. And because we can believe the same stories, we can cooperate flexibly with huge numbers of strangers.

His favourite example is the French car maker Peugeot. Peugeot is not its factories, which could burn down, or its workers, who could all be replaced, or its managers. Peugeot is a legal fiction, a limited liability company, that exists because lawyers performed the right rituals and because millions of people agree to act as if it is real. Nations, human rights, money and gods are, in Harari's language, imagined orders. That does not mean they are lies or unimportant. It means they exist in the shared imagination, and they are astonishingly powerful.

For anyone running a business this is not abstract. A limited company, an authorisation from a regulator, a brand name, a loan agreement: every one of these is a story that holds because enough people keep believing it. Harari's point is that this is the human superpower. Chimpanzees cannot form a company of ten thousand members. We can, because we can share a fiction.
ch.cap: Strangers' shared belief holds up the company's lion

b: The second revolution is the one Harari is most provocative about. The usual story says farming was progress: settled villages, surplus food, leisure, civilisation. Harari calls the Agricultural Revolution history's biggest fraud.

His case is that the average farmer worked harder than the average forager, ate a narrower and worse diet, suffered more disease from living close to animals and to each other, and faced famine when a single crop failed. Skeletons from early farming communities often show more signs of strain and malnutrition than those of hunter-gatherers. So why did anyone do it? Because nobody chose it as a whole. Each small step, a little more wheat here, a slightly larger village there, made sense at the time, and by the time the trap was obvious there was no going back, because there were now too many people to feed by foraging.

He turns the usual picture inside out with a famous flourish. We did not domesticate wheat, he says, wheat domesticated us. A wild grass from a small region of the Middle East persuaded a clever primate to clear forests, carry water and pull weeds for it, until it covered vast stretches of the planet. Measured in copies of its DNA, wheat won. Measured in the happiness of individual humans, Harari is far less sure that we did.

Harari adds a sharper name for the mechanism: the luxury trap. Each convenience that makes life a little easier soon becomes the new normal, and then a necessity people feel they cannot live without. Farmers wanted a little more security and ended up working harder to protect it. He suggests the same thing happens to us today, when a labour-saving device simply raises the amount of work everyone is expected to get through.
ch.cap: A weary farmer stoops to serve the towering wheat

b: Once humans were farming, the next question was how millions of strangers could be fitted into the same order. Harari picks out three great unifiers.

The first is money, which he calls the most universal and most efficient system of mutual trust ever devised. A coin has almost no value in itself. People accept it because they trust that others will, and that trust lets a Christian and a Muslim, who agree on very little, trade happily. The second is empire. Harari refuses the easy judgement that empires were simply wicked. They were often brutal, but they also mixed cultures, spread languages and ideas, and created most of the shared world we inherited. The third is universal religion, and here he includes modern ideologies like liberalism, communism and nationalism, which he treats as religions without gods.

This is where many readers feel the floor move. Harari insists that human rights, too, are an imagined order. There is no organ in the body labelled rights, he argues. That is not a call to abandon them. It is a reminder that they last only as long as people keep choosing to believe in them and defend them.

He also tells the story of writing, and it is not the romantic one. The earliest writing, from Sumer in what is now Iraq, was not poetry or prayer. It was accounting: clay tablets recording barley, taxes, debts and rations. One of the oldest names we can read on such a tablet, Kushim, may belong to an administrator signing off a stock of barley. Writing, in Harari's telling, was invented so that kings and temples could keep track of who owed what, and it made large bureaucracies possible.
ch.cap: A Sumerian clerk tallies barley on a clay tablet

b: The third revolution began around five hundred years ago in Europe, and Harari locates its spark in a surprising place: admitting that we do not know. Medieval scholars believed that everything important was already in scripture or the ancient texts. The new science began with the opposite assumption, that much remained to be discovered, and that observation and mathematics could find it.

He points to the maps. Older maps filled unknown regions with monsters and guesses. Early modern European maps began leaving blank spaces, and those blanks were an invitation. Science, empire and capitalism then fed each other. Explorers carried naturalists, naturalists served empires, and investors funded voyages on credit, trusting that the future would be richer than the present. That trust in future growth, Harari argues, is the engine of the modern economy.

He ends the historical sweep with an uncomfortable question. We are vastly more powerful than our ancestors, but are we happier? He reviews the research on wellbeing, notes that much of happiness depends on expectations and biochemistry, and nods back to his meditation cushion: perhaps the deepest freedom lies not in getting what we want but in understanding our wanting. And he closes by warning that biotechnology and computing may soon let Sapiens redesign itself, which became the subject of his next book, Homo Deus.
ch.cap: A mapmaker leaves the unknown world blank

b: Sapiens is a brilliant read, and you should know clearly where specialists push back, because they push back a good deal.

Many archaeologists reject the idea of a sudden Cognitive Revolution. In a well-known paper in 2000, Sally McBrearty and Alison Brooks argued that modern behaviour, such as making ornaments and using pigments, appeared gradually in Africa over hundreds of thousands of years, not in a single burst seventy thousand years ago. Evidence has since grown that Neanderthals also made symbolic objects, which weakens the claim that only Sapiens could imagine. The anthropologist Christopher Hallpike called the book infotainment, entertaining but careless, and the philosopher Galen Strawson criticised it for sweeping claims stated with more confidence than the evidence allows. Others have accused Harari of presenting speculation, for instance about gossip or about forager happiness, as settled fact.

The agricultural fraud thesis is also contested. Some archaeologists agree farming brought worse health at first. Others argue that the picture varies hugely by region and that foragers were not living in a lost paradise. Harari himself describes his work as a set of big questions rather than a textbook, and the fairest way to read it is that way: a framework for thinking, not a final verdict.

So take the shape, and treat the details with care. The idea that human cooperation runs on shared stories is powerful and widely accepted in some form. The precise dates, the neat revolutions and the confident judgements about ancient happiness are where you should keep your own scepticism switched on.
ch.cap: Archaeologists unearth beads that blur the neat revolution

ch.h: The story you choose to believe
b: It is worth coming back to the boy in Haifa and the man on the cushion, because they explain why Sapiens landed the way it did. Harari is not mainly an archaeologist or a biologist. He is a historian of how people tell stories, trained on soldiers' memoirs, who learned to watch his own mind invent narratives and then turned that gaze on the whole species.

Harari went on to write Homo Deus in 2016, about humanity's possible future, Twenty One Lessons for the Twenty First Century in 2018, and Nexus in 2024, about information networks and artificial intelligence. He became a regular guest at gatherings like the World Economic Forum in Davos, still meditating for hours each day, still describing himself first as a historian.

The lasting gift of the book is a habit of noticing. When you look at your company, your currency, your country or your sense of what is normal, you can ask: is this a physical fact, or an agreement that holds only as long as people keep it? Neither answer makes the thing less real. But knowing which is which tells you what is fragile, what can be changed, and what needs to be maintained by the daily work of keeping people's trust.
ch.cap: Harari watches a city held together by stories

take: Your business is a shared story
A company, a brand and a licence exist because people agree to act as if they do. Protect that agreement with consistency and honesty, because it is the asset everything else rests on.
Strangers cooperate when they share a believable story. A clear mission and transparent rules let customers and staff trust you without knowing you personally.
Farming won through small sensible steps nobody chose as a whole. Check whether a string of reasonable decisions is locking you into more work for less reward.
Its value lies in everyone else accepting it. In any market, reliability of payment and promise is worth more than a clever offer.
Admit what you do not know
Modern science began by leaving blank spaces on the map. Name the gaps in your knowledge and go looking, instead of filling them with confident guesses.
Humanity gained enormous capability without obvious gains in contentment. Ask what growth is for before chasing more of it.
Harari credits meditation with showing him how much of reality is commentary. A few quiet minutes a day can separate events from the stories you tell about them.
Sapiens offers a useful framework with contested details. Borrow the shape of an argument and check the facts before you build on them.

words: Existing because many minds share a belief in it, rather than in the physical world or in one person's head.
Harari's imagined orders, such as money, nations and the Peugeot company, are intersubjective realities that last only while enough people keep believing in them.
Treating an abstract idea as if it were a solid, physical thing.
We reify Peugeot when we talk about it as if it were its factories, when Harari shows it is really a legal fiction held up by shared agreement.
The blending of different beliefs, cultures or traditions into a new combined whole.
Harari credits empires with a kind of syncretism, mixing languages, ideas and customs into much of the shared world we inherited.
Relating to pleasure and the feeling of happiness.
Harari's luxury trap is a hedonic story: each new comfort quickly feels normal, so humanity grew more powerful without obviously growing happier.

We like to imagine that writing was invented for poetry, prayer or love letters. Harari tells a less romantic story. The earliest writing, pressed into clay tablets in ancient Sumer in what is now Iraq, was mostly accounting: barley, taxes, debts and rations. One of the oldest personal names anyone can read on such a tablet is Kushim, which may belong to an administrator signing off a stock of barley, though scholars are not certain it is a person's name at all. So the first name in recorded history could be a bookkeeper's. Writing, in Harari's telling, was invented so that kings and temples could keep track of who owed what.

Early farmers often worked harder than foragers, ate a narrower diet and suffered more disease, and their skeletons show it. Nobody chose this as a plan. Archaeologists still argue about how bleak early farming really was.
biz: Guard the shared story you trade on

Ruby Holdings, HomeownersLoan, Apply4Loan and your FCA authorisation are all imagined orders: they work because customers and lenders believe in them. Inconsistency erodes that belief faster than anything. This week, list every place a customer meets you: Google, Bing and Facebook ads, both websites, WhatsApp templates and call scripts. Check each one gives the same company name, FRN 763879, the same clear statement that you are a broker not a lender, and the required risk warning. Count the mismatches and fix them. Then track one trust measure, such as the share of enquiries that reply to your first WhatsApp message.

Farming won through small sensible steps that nobody chose as a whole, and Harari says modern conveniences do the same. Every new lead source, form tool, bot, tracker or spreadsheet you add makes sense on the day and then becomes something you must maintain forever. This week, write down every recurring task added across both businesses in the last six months, with the hours each takes per week. Set that beside what it produced: completed loans for the brokerage, and properly advised clients for Debt Support Direct. Anything costing hours without moving those outcomes is a candidate to switch off, before it becomes part of the furniture.
connects: Both books treat the switch to farming as the hinge of human history, though Diamond explains why it began where it did while Harari asks whether it made individual people happier.
Harari's money as a system of mutual trust between strangers builds on Adam Smith's picture of trade and the division of labour binding people who never meet.
McKee explains how stories grip an audience, and Harari argues that shared stories are what let millions of strangers cooperate at all.
recap:
Picture a clever boy in Haifa, in northern Israel, who reads everything and asks why about all of it. That boy is Yuval Noah Harari. He grows up to study medieval soldiers and their memoirs at Oxford, a narrow, specialised subject that nobody would expect to produce a global bestseller. Then, in the year two thousand, a friend persuades him to spend ten days in total silence on a meditation retreat. He comes out startled by how much of what he took for reality was really commentary his own mind had added. He has meditated for around two hours a day ever since.

Back in Jerusalem, as a young lecturer, he is handed the job nobody senior wants: teaching the whole of world history to first year students. So he stops asking what happened and starts asking what mattered. That course becomes Sapiens.

The first big idea is that humans were once unremarkable animals, one of several human species, somewhere in the middle of the food chain. Our ancestors pulled ahead, Harari argues, through language, and above all through the ability to talk about things that do not exist.

That is the second idea, and the heart of the book. Nations, money, human rights and companies are imagined orders. The car maker Peugeot is not its factories or its staff. It is a legal fiction that millions of people agree to treat as real. Imagined does not mean fake. It means it lives in our shared belief, and that shared belief lets strangers cooperate in their millions.

The third idea is the most provocative. Farming, Harari says, was history's biggest fraud. Farmers worked harder and ate worse than foragers, and nobody chose it as a whole. Small sensible steps added up to a trap. We did not domesticate wheat. Wheat domesticated us.

The fourth is that money, empires and universal religions knitted humanity together, and that modern science began with a confession: we do not know. Blank spaces on the map became an invitation.

And the fifth is a caution about the book itself. Archaeologists dispute the idea of a sudden mental revolution seventy thousand years ago, and critics say Harari states speculation with too much confidence. Take the shape of his argument, and keep your own judgement switched on for the details.

So when you look at your company, your currency or your country, ask one quiet question, the one Harari learned on the cushion. Is this a fact of the world, or a story we keep alive together? Here is the line to remember: the things that matter most are often the ones that exist only because we keep believing in them.
